label: prf:hyperelliptic-z5-classification
title: Proof of hyperelliptic z5 classification
html:
Proof. Proof of hyperelliptic z5 classification

Proof. Because \phi commutes with \iota, it descends along \pi to an automorphism \bar\phi of \mathbb{P}^1. Faithfulness of \phi and commutativity with \iota force \bar\phi to be an element of order 5 in \mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{C}) = \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^1). Every order-5 element of \mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{C}) is conjugate to x \mapsto \zeta_5 x. This map has exactly two fixed points on \mathbb{P}^1, namely \{0, \infty\}. Under Möbius normalisation, we set \bar\phi \colon x \mapsto \zeta_5 x.

The orbits of \bar\phi on \mathbb{P}^1 have size 1 (fixed points: 0, \infty) or 5 (generic orbits \{a, \zeta_5 a, \zeta_5^2 a, \zeta_5^3 a, \zeta_5^4 a\} for a \notin \{0, \infty\}).

Since \phi commutes with \iota, the branch divisor of \pi is \phi-invariant. It descends to a \bar\phi-invariant subset of \mathbb{P}^1. Its cardinality is a non-negative combination of 1 and 5:

  |\mathrm{Branch}(\pi)| \in \{0, 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12, \ldots\}.

Riemann–Hurwitz gives:

  |\mathrm{Branch}(\pi)| = 2g(X) + 2.

The size is even. Condition (ii) forces g \geq 2. A sphere has \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{P}^1) = \mathrm{PGL}_2 which admits \mathbb{Z}_5, but a sphere is excluded from the hyperelliptic indexing g \geq 2. Thus, the size is at least 6. The smallest admissible |\mathrm{Branch}(\pi)| in our list that is even and at least 6 is exactly 6. This implies g = 2.

A \bar\phi-invariant set of size 6 decomposes uniquely into one size-5 orbit and one fixed point. (No other solution to 6 = 5a + b exists for a, b \geq 0 and b \leq 2.) The branch divisor is therefore:

  \mathrm{Branch}(\pi) = \{\zeta_5^k a : 0 \leq k \leq 4\} \cup \{c\} \qquad \text{for some } a \neq 0, c \in \{0, \infty\}.

After the rescaling x \mapsto a^{-1} x, we set a = 1. This yields the orbit \{1, \zeta_5, \zeta_5^2, \zeta_5^3, \zeta_5^4\}. The two choices c = \infty and c = 0 yield the equations y^2 = x^5 - 1 and y^2 = x(x^5 - 1) = x^6 - x, respectively. The change of chart x \mapsto 1/x, y \mapsto y/x^3 maps one to the other up to a sign. We absorb this sign into y. Since the branch divisor determines a smooth hyperelliptic curve of genus \geq 2 up to isomorphism, both choices yield isomorphic curves.

Therefore, X \cong \mathcal{X}_5. \square
